nodes.label: Ottoman Iraq: the Three Provinces
nodes.full: What precedes: the Mamluk regime, the frontier province, the tribal south turning Shia, Baghdad reviving, and the British Residency established at Baghdad. See iraq-1534-1831.
nodes.src: background — see the folio iraq-1534-1831.

nodes.label: British Iraq and the Kingdom
nodes.full: The aftermath: the two-year Mesopotamian campaign, the Mandate, the Kingdom of Iraq welded from the three vilayets, the Hashemite monarchy, and the Ottoman-trained officers in power. See iraq-1914-1958.
nodes.src: background — see the folio iraq-1914-1958.

nodes.label: The Ottoman Empire and the Tanzimat
nodes.full: The reforming imperial state at Istanbul — the Tanzimat edicts, the vilayet law, the 1858 Land Code, the state schools and courts, and then the Young Turks; the centre whose reforms remade Iraq.
nodes.src: background — Roderic Davison, 'Reform in the Ottoman Empire' (1963).

nodes.label: Britain and the Empire of India
nodes.full: The East India Company and then the Raj — the road to India, the Gulf forward policy, the Lynch steamers, the Baghdad Residency, the oil interest, and the archaeology and the museums.
nodes.src: background — J. B. Kelly, 'Britain and the Persian Gulf' (1968); Marian Kent, 'Oil and Empire' (1976).

nodes.label: Qajar Iran and the Shia world
nodes.full: The Shia monarchy across the border — the tobacco concession and its cancellation, the Constitutional Revolution, the pilgrim traffic and the corpse caravans, and the Persian consul in the shrine cities.
nodes.src: background — Nikki Keddie, 'Qajar Iran and the Rise of Reza Khan' (1999).

nodes.label: Direct rule and the first reformers
nodes.full: With the Mamluk regime gone, Istanbul governed Iraq directly again through appointed pashas — Ali Riza, Najib, Namık — who brought the first instalments of the Tanzimat: conscription, a land tax, a nizamiye army, the beginnings of a bureaucracy. It was resisted at every step. Najib Pasha's storm of autonomous Karbala in 1843 showed how the reformed state meant to impose itself.
nodes.src: Ebubekir Ceylan, 'The Ottoman Origins of Modern Iraq' (2011); Gökhan Çetinsaya, 'The Ottoman Administration of Iraq, 1890–1908' (2006).

nodes.label: Midhat Pasha and the Tanzimat in full
nodes.full: In three years Midhat Pasha remade the province. He applied the new vilayet law and the 1858 Land Code, set up provincial and municipal councils, raised a conscript army, opened schools, a hospital and an industrial school, started the first Iraqi newspaper and a river-steamer company, tore down Baghdad's walls, settled tribal land, and pushed Ottoman control down the Gulf coast to al-Hasa. No other governor did as much, for good and ill.
nodes.src: Ali Haydar Midhat, 'The Life of Midhat Pasha' (1903); Ebubekir Ceylan (2011).

nodes.label: The three vilayets and the notable families
nodes.full: Iraq settled into three provinces — Baghdad, Basra (formally separate from 1884), Mosul — under a rotating cast of governors, some able, most not. The lasting winners were the urban notable families — the Naqibs, Gaylanis, Suwaydis, Pachachis, Chalabis — who filled the council seats and the official posts and used the Land Code to become the province's landlords. A provincial oligarchy took shape.
nodes.src: Gökhan Çetinsaya, 'The Ottoman Administration of Iraq, 1890–1908' (2006); Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes' (1978).

nodes.label: The Young Turks and the eve of war
nodes.full: The 1908 revolution restored the constitution, sent Iraqi deputies to a real parliament, and let a free press explode into being. But the Committee of Union and Progress governed with a centralising, Turkifying hand that pushed the Arab notables toward opposition and the Arab officers toward conspiracy. By 1914 Iraq had a nationalist underground and a resentful elite, and a British army in the Gulf.
nodes.src: Hasan Kayalı, 'Arabs and Young Turks' (1997); Reeva Simon, 'Iraq Between the Two World Wars' (1986), on the officer background.

nodes.label: The tribal shaykhs made landlords
nodes.full: The 1858 Land Code let land be registered as private property, and across the tribal south it was registered overwhelmingly in the names of the paramount shaykhs. A man who had been a leader among kinsmen became a landowner over tenants; the tribesman became a sharecropper. The Sa'dun, the shaykhs of the Al bu Muhammad, the Bani Lam and the rest moved to town houses and drew rents. A new rural class order was born.
nodes.src: Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes and the Revolutionary Movements of Iraq' (1978); Albertine Jwaideh, 'Midhat Pasha and the Land System of Lower Iraq' (1963).

nodes.label: The shrine cities and the marjaiyya
nodes.full: Najaf and Karbala went on governing themselves, under the senior mujtahids, the shrine custodians, the Persian consul and the armed neighbourhood factions. Over the century the office of a single supreme source of emulation, the marjaʿ al-taqlīd, took form there, and with it a clergy the Ottoman state could not command — as the Tobacco Protest of 1891 and the Iranian revolution after 1905 both showed.
nodes.src: Meir Litvak, 'Shiʿi Scholars of Nineteenth-Century Iraq' (1998); Yitzhak Nakash, 'The Shiʿis of Iraq' (1994).

nodes.label: The desert, al-Hasa and Kuwait
nodes.full: South and west of the settled land the powers were the Rashidi emirate of Ha'il, the reviving Al Saud, and the fading Muntafiq. Midhat Pasha's forces took al-Hasa in 1871, planting Ottoman garrisons on the Gulf coast; Kuwait under Mubarak al-Sabah slipped free, signing a protection deal with Britain in 1899; and in 1913 Ibn Saud swept the Ottomans out of al-Hasa altogether.
nodes.src: Frederick Anscombe, 'The Ottoman Gulf' (1997); J. B. Kelly, 'Britain and the Persian Gulf' (1968).

nodes.label: The Arab officers and the nationalists
nodes.full: A cohort of young men from Baghdad and Mosul families went through the Ottoman military academies and came back reading nationalist pamphlets. In 1913 the officer al-Misri founded al-ʿAhd, a secret society of Arab officers; the Arab Congress met in Paris the same year. Among the Iraqi members were Nuri al-Saʿid, Jaʿfar al-ʿAskari and Yasin al-Hashimi — the men who would change sides in the coming war and rule the country after it.
nodes.src: Reeva Simon, 'Iraq Between the Two World Wars: The Militarist Origins of Tyranny' (1986); Eliezer Tauber, 'The Emergence of the Arab Movements' (1993).

nodes.label: The Ottoman sack of Karbala
nodes.full: For decades Karbala had been ruled by its shrine factions and the gangs, with the Ottoman governor shut out. In January 1843 Najib Pasha stormed the city to bring it to heel, and his troops killed thousands — figures run from three to five thousand — in the streets and the sanctuary. It broke the city's autonomy and announced that the reformed state would not tolerate ungoverned space, even holy ground.
nodes.src: Juan Cole & Moojan Momen, 'Mafia, Mob and Shiism in Iraq: The Rebellion of Ottoman Karbala 1824–1843' (1986).

nodes.label: The wars of conscription and the land tax
nodes.full: The Tanzimat state's new demands — draft the young men, register and tax the land, disarm the tribe — meant war across the countryside for two generations. The Yazidis of Sinjar rose and were massacred; the Shammar, the mid-Euphrates tribes and the marsh confederations fought the tax columns again and again. The state won slowly and violently, and the memory of the columns lasted.
nodes.src: Gökhan Çetinsaya, 'The Ottoman Administration of Iraq' (2006); Nelida Fuccaro, 'The Other Kurds: Yazidis in Colonial Iraq' (1999), on Sinjar.

nodes.label: The breaking of the Muntafiq
nodes.full: The Muntafiq of the lower Euphrates, led by the sharifian Sa'dun family, were often stronger than the pasha. Midhat Pasha and his successors set out to end the confederation — deposing and deporting its shaykhs, registering its land, and turning it into an administered district with a governor. The great southern tribal power was dismantled, its shaykhs made into rival landlords, and the ground prepared for the revolts of 1915 and 1920.
nodes.src: Albertine Jwaideh, 'Midhat Pasha and the Land System of Lower Iraq' (1963); Hala Fattah, 'The Politics of Regional Trade' (1997).

nodes.label: The desert wars of Ibn Rashid and Ibn Saud
nodes.full: In the deep desert the Rashidi emirs of Ha'il and the exiled and then reviving Al Saud fought for Najd, both drawing the Ottomans and the Iraqi tribes into the struggle. The Saudis' defeat at Mulayda in 1891 drove them to Kuwait; Ibn Saud's recapture of Riyadh in 1902 began the state that would take al-Hasa from the Ottomans in 1913 and, in time, most of Arabia.
nodes.src: Alexei Vassiliev, 'The History of Saudi Arabia' (2000); Madawi al-Rasheed, 'A History of Saudi Arabia' (2002).

nodes.label: Najaf and the Iranian Constitutional Revolution
nodes.full: When Iran rose for a constitution, the leading mujtahids of Najaf — Akhund Khurasani, Mazandarani, Tehrani — put the marjaʿiyya behind it, issuing fatwas, sheltering activists, and turning the shrine cities into a command centre of the Iranian revolution across the border. It was the clearest demonstration yet that the Najaf clergy were a political power with reach far beyond Iraq.
nodes.src: Abdul-Hadi Hairi, 'Shiʿism and Constitutionalism in Iran' (1977); Meir Litvak (1998).

nodes.label: The British landing at Basra
nodes.full: On the outbreak of war an Anglo-Indian force landed at Fao on 6 November 1914, brushed aside the Ottoman defenders, and took Basra on the 22nd — sent to protect the oil pipeline and the head of the Gulf. It was the first move of a campaign that would grind up the Tigris to Kut and Baghdad over the next three years and end four centuries of Ottoman Iraq.
nodes.src: Charles Townshend, 'When God Made Hell: The British Invasion of Mesopotamia' (2010); A. J. Barker, 'The First Iraq War' (2009).

nodes.label: The Tanzimat state comes to Iraq
nodes.full: Over half a century a bureaucratic state replaced the pasha's household: the vilayet with its provincial and district councils, the nizamiye courts alongside the sharia courts, a conscript army, state primary and secondary schools, a census, a land registry, a post and a telegraph. It reached unevenly and was resented, but by 1900 Iraq had the apparatus of a modern province — thin, but real.
nodes.src: Gökhan Çetinsaya, 'The Ottoman Administration of Iraq, 1890–1908' (2006); Ebubekir Ceylan (2011).

nodes.label: The 1858 Land Code and the landlord class
nodes.full: The Ottoman Land Code let cultivated land be registered as private property. Across tribal Iraq the registration went to the paramount shaykhs and the town notables, converting collective tribal territory into private estates and the tribesmen who worked it into sharecroppers. It created, within two generations, a landlord class and a landless peasantry where neither had existed — the deepest single change of the century, and a wound in Iraqi society that ran to 1958.
nodes.src: Albertine Jwaideh, 'Midhat Pasha and the Land System of Lower Iraq' (1963); Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes' (1978); the Ottoman Land Code of 1858.

nodes.label: The three vilayets and the notable oligarchy
nodes.full: Baghdad, Basra and Mosul became administrative provinces run through councils and salaried officials — and the councils and the offices were captured by a small set of urban families. The same names appear as council members, judges, tax officials, deputies and, thanks to the Land Code, the largest landowners. This provincial oligarchy, Ottoman-made, would furnish the politicians of the monarchy after 1921.
nodes.src: Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes' (1978); Gökhan Çetinsaya (2006).

nodes.label: The shrine cities under the clergy
nodes.full: Even after the sack of Karbala, Najaf and Karbala ran largely on their own terms. Real power lay with the senior mujtahids, the shrine treasurers, the Persian consul, and the armed neighbourhood factions — the Zuqurt and the Shumurt of Najaf — who fought over the pilgrim trade. The marjaʿiyya's independent income from the religious tithe made it an authority the state had to court rather than command.
nodes.src: Yitzhak Nakash, 'The Shiʿis of Iraq' (1994); Meir Litvak (1998).

nodes.label: The millet communities in the reform era
nodes.full: The 1856 reform edict promised the non-Muslims legal equality and set them to reorganising: the Jews of Baghdad elected a chief rabbi and a lay communal council and opened modern schools; the Chaldean, Syriac and Armenian churches kept their own courts and schools; and the new category of the Ottoman citizen was laid over the old status of the dhimmi. In practice the change was partial and the old order persisted underneath.
nodes.src: Bruce Masters, 'Christians and Jews in the Ottoman Arab World' (2001); Zvi Yehuda, 'The New Babylonian Diaspora' (2017).

nodes.label: The end of the Kurdish emirates
nodes.full: The Ottoman state that reasserted itself in Iraq also broke the last self-governing Kurdish principalities — Soran under the Mir of Rawanduz, then Bahdinan, then Baban, all abolished by mid-century. Direct rule never really replaced them; into the vacuum stepped the Naqshbandi shaykhly families — the Barzinji, the Talabani, the Barzani — and Shaykh Ubaydullah's cross-border rising of 1880 was the first stirring of a Kurdish national idea.
nodes.src: Martin van Bruinessen, 'Agha, Shaikh and State: The Social and Political Structures of Kurdistan' (1992); Hakan Özoğlu, 'Kurdish Notables and the Ottoman State' (2004).

nodes.label: The single source of emulation
nodes.full: The Usuli doctrine that the layman must follow a living mujtahid was carried a step further: by mid-century Murtada al-Ansari was recognised as the first sole marjaʿ al-taqlīd, the one jurist whose rulings all should follow. The office, the ranking of scholars beneath him, and the flow of the religious tithe to his hands, matured over the following decades, and Najaf settled its primacy over Karbala as the seminary of the Shia world.
nodes.src: Meir Litvak, 'Shiʿi Scholars of Nineteenth-Century Iraq' (1998); Ahmad Kazemi Moussavi, 'Religious Authority in Shiʿite Islam' (1996).

nodes.label: The Tobacco Protest
nodes.full: When the Shah of Iran sold a British company a monopoly over the whole Iranian tobacco trade, the marjaʿ resident at Samarra, Mirza Hasan Shirazi, issued a one-line fatwa declaring the use of tobacco to be war against the Hidden Imam. The boycott was total — the Shah's own household gave up smoking — and the concession was cancelled. It was the first proof that a ruling from the shrine cities could move an entire nation.
nodes.src: Nikki Keddie, 'Religion and Rebellion in Iran: The Tobacco Protest of 1891–1892' (1966).

nodes.label: The Najaf ulama and the Iranian revolution
nodes.full: The Constitutional Revolution in Iran split the Shia clergy, and its most powerful backers sat in Najaf: Akhund Khurasani and his colleagues issued fatwas for the constitution, corresponded with the deputies in Tehran, and made the shrine cities a safe base and a nerve centre for the movement. The episode forced open the deep question of whether the rule of a qualified jurist and an elected assembly could be reconciled.
nodes.src: Abdul-Hadi Hairi, 'Shiʿism and Constitutionalism in Iran' (1977).

nodes.label: The Jews of Baghdad at their height
nodes.full: By 1900 Jews were perhaps a quarter of Baghdad's people — the largest single community — and dominant in its trade, its banking and its bazaar. The Alliance Israélite schools, opened from 1864, turned out a French-literate professional and commercial class; the yeshivas kept up the old learning; the great houses ran branches to Bombay and Shanghai. It was the community's golden age, and it had about fifty years left.
nodes.src: Nissim Rejwan, 'The Jews of Iraq: 3000 Years of History and Culture' (1985); Orit Bashkin, 'New Babylonians' (2012).

nodes.label: The missions, the schools and the churches
nodes.full: The Dominican mission at Mosul ran a press from 1857; American and other Protestant missions opened schools; the Alliance and the Ottoman state added more. Education widened, and with it a new Christian and Jewish intelligentsia. The Chaldean Catholic Church consolidated its hold over most of the old Church of the East. On the margins the Yazidis of Sinjar continued to be raided as heretics.
nodes.src: Bruce Masters, 'Christians and Jews in the Ottoman Arab World' (2001); David Wilmshurst, 'The Martyred Church' (2011).

nodes.label: The press and the birth of public opinion
nodes.full: Midhat Pasha founded al-Zawra' in 1869, the first newspaper printed in Iraq — an official gazette, in Ottoman Turkish and Arabic. After the Young Turk revolution of 1908 lifted the censorship, dozens of private papers appeared in Baghdad, Basra, Mosul and Najaf, arguing politics in Arabic for a widening readership. An Iraqi public opinion, and an Iraqi political vocabulary, came into being in these years.
nodes.src: ʿAbd al-Razzaq al-Hasani, 'Ta'rīkh al-Ṣiḥāfa al-ʿIrāqiyya' (1957); Orit Bashkin, 'The Other Iraq' (2009).

nodes.label: al-Zahawi, al-Rusafi and modern Arabic poetry
nodes.full: Two Baghdadis, Jamil Sidqi al-Zahawi and Maʿruf al-Rusafi, carried Arabic poetry in Iraq from the ornate neo-classical style toward the social and political: verse about the veil and the schoolhouse, tyranny and reform, science and the nation. Both sat in the Ottoman parliament after 1908. They are the founders of the modern Iraqi poetic tradition that would run through al-Jawahiri to al-Sayyab.
nodes.src: Salma Khadra Jayyusi, 'Trends and Movements in Modern Arabic Poetry' (1977); the 'Dīwān' of al-Rusafi.

nodes.label: The Assyrian excavations
nodes.full: Austen Henry Layard's digs at Nimrud and Nineveh in the 1840s and 50s pulled the winged bulls and the palace reliefs and the library of Ashurbanipal — thirty thousand tablets — out of the mounds and shipped them to the British Museum. George Smith found the Babylonian flood story among them in 1872. Then came the German excavation of Babylon and Assur and the American dig at Nippur. The material of ancient Iraq was carried off to the museums of the West.
nodes.src: Mogens Trolle Larsen, 'The Conquest of Assyria: Excavations in an Antique Land' (1996).

nodes.label: The building and unbuilding of Baghdad
nodes.full: Midhat Pasha tore down the medieval walls and the citadel and laid the first straight streets; he and later governors built the Sarai, the hospital, the industrial school, a clock tower, barracks and offices in a mixed Ottoman-European provincial manner. The great sites were still the shrines — Kazimayn, Najaf and Karbala re-gilded again with Iranian and Indian money — but the city was starting to acquire the look of a modern provincial capital.
nodes.src: Caecilia Pieri, 'Baghdad Arts Deco' background; the Ottoman-era Baghdad in the Iraqi architectural surveys.

nodes.label: The Iraqi maqam and the coffee-house
nodes.full: The maqam al-ʿIraqi — a suite of classical sung poetry, each maqam a fixed sequence of modes and rhythms — took its mature form in the coffee-houses of Baghdad, sung by masters like Ahmad Zaidan and Rashid al-Qundarchi to the chalghi ensemble of santur, spike-fiddle and drums. The instrumentalists were very largely Jewish. The café was where urban culture happened, and the maqam was its highest art.
nodes.src: Scheherazade Qassim Hassan, 'Les instruments de musique en Irak' (1980); the maqām recordings and studies of the Chalghi Baghdadi.

nodes.label: The Usuli clerical sciences at Najaf
nodes.full: The Najaf seminary matured into a self-governing intellectual institution with a settled curriculum. Murtada al-Ansari's works on legal theory and on transactions became the standard advanced texts — they are still taught there — and the great teaching circles debated how the authority of a qualified jurist should work in an age of constitutions, parliaments and mass politics. The hawza thought about power because it now had some.
nodes.src: al-Ansari, 'Farāʾid al-Uṣūl' (al-Rasāʾil) and 'al-Makāsib'; Robert Gleave and Meir Litvak on the Najaf curriculum.

nodes.label: Ottoman modern learning and the officer class
nodes.full: Beside the Quran school, the maktab, the Ottoman state built the mekteb — secondary schools and, for the ablest, the military and civil academies of Istanbul — teaching Turkish, mathematics, French, geography and the ideas of the century. Out of them came a generation of Iraqi officers and officials, at home in the modern world and, increasingly, in Arab nationalism. The split between the two kinds of school ran through Iraqi society.
nodes.src: Reeva Simon, 'Iraq Between the Two World Wars' (1986); Benjamin Fortna, 'Imperial Classroom' (2002).

nodes.label: The Nahda reaches Iraq
nodes.full: The Arabic cultural revival — the Nahda — arrived through the books and journals of Cairo and Beirut and the salons of Baghdad and Basra: Islamic reformism (al-Afghani taught briefly in the shrine cities; ʿAbduh's ideas circulated), Arab cultural pride, constitutionalism, popular science. A reading public formed around the new papers and the private libraries, and the questions that would preoccupy twentieth-century Iraq were first argued here.
nodes.src: Orit Bashkin, 'The Other Iraq: Pluralism and Culture in Hashemite Iraq' (2009); Albert Hourani, 'Arabic Thought in the Liberal Age' (1962).

nodes.label: Assyriology, born from Iraqi soil
nodes.full: Henry Rawlinson's copying of the trilingual cliff at Behistun, and the work of Hincks and Oppert, cracked cuneiform in the 1850s, and a whole new discipline followed — reading the Assyrian annals, the Babylonian chronicles, the flood story, the code of Hammurabi. It was built entirely on tablets dug out of Iraq, and it was done almost entirely in the universities and museums of Europe, by scholars who mostly never came.
nodes.src: Kevin Cathcart (ed.), 'The Correspondence of Edward Hincks'; Mogens Trolle Larsen, 'The Conquest of Assyria' (1996).

nodes.label: Iraq joins the world economy
nodes.full: Steam navigation and the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 turned Iraq from a caravan land facing inward to an exporting one facing the sea. Grain, dates, wool and liquorice went out in rising quantity; Basra grew into a modern port; land values climbed. A peripheral, largely subsistence economy was pulled into global trade within a single generation — with all the dislocation that implied.
nodes.src: Charles Issawi, 'The Fertile Crescent 1800–1914' (1988); Hala Fattah, 'The Politics of Regional Trade' (1997).

nodes.label: The steamers and the telegraph
nodes.full: From 1861 the Lynch brothers' British firm ran a steamer monopoly up the Tigris, alongside the Ottoman line, and the telegraph reached from Baghdad to Fao as a link in the Indo-European cable to India. Journeys that had taken weeks took days; orders and news moved in hours. The compression of distance was what made both central government control and world-market trade possible in Iraq at all.
nodes.src: Marion Kent, 'Oil and Empire' background; Roderic Davison, 'The Advent of the Electric Telegraph in the Ottoman Empire' (1990).

nodes.label: The date economy of Basra
nodes.full: The date gardens along the Shatt al-Arab made Basra the world's leading date exporter. British and American buyers set up packing houses; the Basra date became a global commodity sold by the pound in London and New York. Behind the trade was a sharecropping labour system and a fragile monoculture vulnerable to the red palm weevil, the salt tide and the market.
nodes.src: Charles Issawi, 'The Fertile Crescent 1800–1914' (1988); the date-trade material in the British consular reports.

nodes.label: The land boom and the sarkal system
nodes.full: Rising export prices and the 1858 registration made Iraqi farmland worth owning. Shaykhs, town merchants and officials bought and registered it, and a new figure appeared between owner and cultivator: the sarkal, the estate foreman and rent-collector. The fallah's share of his crop fell steadily. The class structure of the Iraqi countryside — big absentee owners, a squeezed peasantry, the sarkal in between — was set in these decades and lasted to the revolution of 1958.
nodes.src: Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes and the Revolutionary Movements of Iraq' (1978); Robert Fernea, 'Shaykh and Effendi' (1970).

nodes.label: The oil that was coming
nodes.full: The oil seeps at Baba Gurgur near Kirkuk and around Mosul had burned for millennia. Now they mattered: D'Arcy struck oil in neighbouring Persia in 1908, and the Ottoman government, the Deutsche Bank and Anglo-Dutch and British interests fought over a concession for Mosul, incorporating the Turkish Petroleum Company in 1912. The resource that would define twentieth-century Iraq was being carved up before a single well was drilled.
nodes.src: Marian Kent, 'Oil and Empire: British Policy and Mesopotamian Oil 1900–1920' (1976); Daniel Yergin, 'The Prize' (1991).

nodes.label: Steam on the rivers and the telegraph line
nodes.full: The paddle steamers of the Lynch and Ottoman lines, with their workshops and coal depots, and the telegraph with its Iraqi operators and repair gangs, were the country's first industrial infrastructure. They were foreign-built and foreign-run, but they trained a small class of Iraqi mechanics and clerks and they changed what the words 'far away' meant.
nodes.src: the Lynch Brothers company records; Ebubekir Ceylan (2011) on infrastructure.

nodes.label: The Baghdad Railway
nodes.full: The German concession of 1903 to build a railway from Anatolia through Baghdad to Basra was the grand symbol of the powers' contest over Iraq — 'Berlin to Baghdad'. By 1914 the line had crossed much of Anatolia, the Taurus tunnels were unfinished, and only the Baghdad–Samarra stretch had opened in the Iraqi plain. The war stopped it half-built, but the route it chose shaped Iraq's later rail map.
nodes.src: Sean McMeekin, 'The Berlin-Baghdad Express' (2010); Marian Kent, 'Oil and Empire' (1976).

nodes.label: Irrigation reborn — the Hindiyya Barrage
nodes.full: Sir William Willcocks, fresh from the Aswan Dam, surveyed the Iraqi rivers and in 1911 published a plan to restore the ancient irrigation and make the Sawad bloom again. The first result was the Hindiyya Barrage, built 1911–13 to control the Euphrates and put water back into the dying Hilla branch. It was the first modern irrigation work in Iraq, and a foretaste of the dams that would follow under the British and the state.
nodes.src: William Willcocks, 'The Irrigation of Mesopotamia' (1911); the Hindiyya Barrage engineering records.

nodes.label: The excavation as an industrial operation
nodes.full: Digging up ancient Iraq was heavy industry: Layard employed hundreds of local workers with picks and baskets, cut colossal sculptures free and floated them down the rivers on rafts. Robert Koldewey at Babylon, from 1899, did it as a science — the careful trench, the recorded section, the first serious excavation of mud-brick architecture — but still with a small army of Iraqi labourers doing the work of the trenches.
nodes.src: Robert Koldewey, 'Das wieder erstehende Babylon' (1913); Mogens Trolle Larsen, 'The Conquest of Assyria' (1996).

nodes.label: The Anglo-Ottoman-German contest for Iraq
nodes.full: By the 1900s Iraq was a prize in the pre-war rivalry of the powers: the German railway concession, the scramble for the Mosul oil, the navigation of the rivers, and the head of the Gulf. Britain pushed a forward policy — protection for Kuwait in 1899, the Anglo-Ottoman conventions of 1913–14 on the Gulf and the boundaries — while Germany pushed the railway and the Ottomans tried to hold the middle.
nodes.src: Stuart Cohen, 'British Policy in Mesopotamia 1903–1914' (1976); Sean McMeekin, 'The Berlin-Baghdad Express' (2010).

nodes.label: The shrine cities and the Iranian revolution
nodes.full: The Najaf clergy's leadership of the Iranian Constitutional Revolution ran on a constant traffic across the border: activists sheltering in the shrine cities, money and pamphlets moving both ways, fatwas telegraphed to Tehran. It confirmed the shrine cities as effectively extraterritorial to Iranian politics, and deepened a clerical connection between Iraq and Iran that no state border would ever quite sever.
nodes.src: Abdul-Hadi Hairi, 'Shiʿism and Constitutionalism in Iran' (1977); Meir Litvak (1998).

nodes.label: The Baghdadi Jewish trading world
nodes.full: The commercial diaspora that began with David Sassoon's flight to Bombay now spanned the British East: houses and families in Calcutta, Rangoon, Singapore, Hong Kong, Shanghai and London, tied by marriage, credit and a Judeo-Arabic press. Baghdad was the mother-community, sending sons out to the branches and drawing back the remittances. Iraqi commercial talent had gone global a lifetime before the country itself opened up.
nodes.src: Joan Roland, 'The Jewish Communities of India' (1998); Chiara Betta on the Baghdadi Jews of Shanghai.

nodes.label: The pilgrimage and the Hajj road
nodes.full: Iraq was the muster point for the Persian and the Shammar hajj caravans crossing the desert to Mecca, and the shrine cities were the year-round destination of the Shia visitation. The Ottoman state invested in the pilgrimage as a claim to Islamic leadership. The caravans also carried cholera, and a network of quarantine stations grew up along the routes — one of the first modern public-health systems in the region.
nodes.src: the Ottoman hajj administration in Selim Deringil, 'The Well-Protected Domains' (1998); the cholera and quarantine literature.

nodes.label: The antiquities trade and the museums
nodes.full: With no effective antiquities law and firmans easy to obtain, the tablets and sculptures of ancient Iraq flowed out steadily — to the British Museum, the Louvre, Berlin and the University of Pennsylvania — through the Baghdad dealers and the excavation shipments. A domestic interest in the Iraqi past was only just beginning; the men who would found the Iraq Museum in the 1920s were students in these years.
nodes.src: Magnus Bernhardsson, 'Reclaiming a Plundered Past: Archaeology and Nation Building in Modern Iraq' (2005).

nodes.label: The making of modern Iraqi society
nodes.full: This is the period that built the social structure the twentieth century inherited: a landlord class of shaykhs and town notables sitting on a mass of sharecropping fallahin; a Shia majority in the countryside and the shrine cities; a Jewish and Christian commercial bourgeoisie in the towns; an Ottoman-schooled officer and official class; and a clergy in Najaf answering to no state. Every later Iraqi conflict runs back through these categories.
nodes.src: Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes and the Revolutionary Movements of Iraq' (1978).

nodes.label: The three vilayets and the country to come
nodes.full: Baghdad, Basra and Mosul were the three provinces the British would weld into the Kingdom of Iraq in 1921 — and the question of whether Mosul, with its Kurds and Turkmen and Christians, belonged with Baghdad at all was already being asked. The map of modern Iraq, and its central unresolved argument about who is in it, were both prefigured in the late-Ottoman administrative order.
nodes.src: Sarah Shields, 'Mosul before Iraq' (2000); Peter Sluglett, 'Britain in Iraq' (2007).

nodes.label: Iraq in the powers' rivalries
nodes.full: The railway, the oil, the rivers and the Gulf pulled Iraq into the Anglo-German-Russian-Ottoman contest of the pre-war years. The very things that made the country valuable to the modern world — the route to India, the untapped oil, the strategic head of the Gulf — were what made it a target in 1914 and a mandate in 1920. Iraq had lost the ability to be left alone.
nodes.src: Stuart Cohen, 'British Policy in Mesopotamia 1903–1914' (1976); Sean McMeekin, 'The Berlin-Baghdad Express' (2010).

nodes.label: The Ottoman order at its end
nodes.full: By late 1914 Iraq had a strained modernising administration, a resentful Arab notable class, a nationalist officer underground, and a British and Indian army coming ashore at Fao. Four centuries of Ottoman Iraq were about to end in a two-and-a-half-year campaign, and the modern state — its borders, its landlords, its officers, its sectarian arithmetic all inherited — would be built on the wreck by the British.
nodes.src: Charles Townshend, 'When God Made Hell' (2010); Toby Dodge, 'Inventing Iraq' (2003).

nodes.label: Midhat Pasha
nodes.full: The reforming governor of Baghdad for three years, architect of the Ottoman vilayet system, later twice grand vizier and the moving force behind the 1876 constitution — and then deposed, exiled, and strangled in a prison at Taif on Sultan Abdulhamid's orders in 1883. He is the type of the Ottoman liberal reformer, and the man whose brief tenure in Iraq did more than any other to shape the modern country, for good and for ill.
nodes.src: Ali Haydar Midhat, 'The Life of Midhat Pasha' (1903); Roderic Davison, 'Reform in the Ottoman Empire 1856–1876' (1963).

nodes.label: The shaykh who became a landlord
nodes.full: A Sa'dun of the Muntafiq, or a shaykh of the Al bu Muhammad, who registered the tribe's land in his own name under the 1858 code, built a house in Basra or Baghdad, sent a son to the Ottoman school, and collected the rent from men who had been his kinsmen and were now his tenants. Multiplied across the confederations, he is how tribal authority in Iraq turned into landed property and a class was born.
nodes.src: Albertine Jwaideh, 'Midhat Pasha and the Land System of Lower Iraq' (1963); Hanna Batatu (1978).

nodes.label: The Alliance schoolboy
nodes.full: A Jewish boy in Baghdad learning French, bookkeeping and the wider world at the Alliance Israélite school, bound for a clerkship in a British firm, a merchant house in Basra, or a branch of the family business in Bombay or Shanghai. He is the making of the modernised Baghdadi Jewish middle class — the most Europeanised, outward-looking element of Iraqi society, and the one with the least time left in the country.
nodes.src: Orit Bashkin, 'New Babylonians: A History of Jews in Modern Iraq' (2012); the Alliance school reports.

nodes.label: The Arab officer
nodes.full: A young man from a Baghdad or Mosul family, trained at the Ottoman war academy in Istanbul, serving in the Balkans or Yemen, reading the nationalist tracts, joining al-ʿAhd. A Nuri al-Saʿid, a Jaʿfar al-ʿAskari, a Yasin al-Hashimi — soon to be captured by or to defect to the British, to fight in the Arab Revolt, and to spend the next thirty years running the Kingdom of Iraq and quarrelling over it.
nodes.src: Reeva Simon, 'Iraq Between the Two World Wars' (1986); Phebe Marr, 'The Modern History of Iraq' (2017).

nodes.label: Hormuzd Rassam and the diggers
nodes.full: A Mosul-born Assyrian Christian who began as Layard's assistant, then ran his own excavations for the British Museum — finding the bronze gates of Balawat and more of the Nineveh library — and was patronised, doubted and cheated by the London establishment as a 'native'. He stands for the Iraqi hands and eyes behind the 'British' discovery of Assyria, and for the thousands of local workers who dug the mounds.
nodes.src: Hormuzd Rassam, 'Asshur and the Land of Nimrod' (1897); Mogens Trolle Larsen, 'The Conquest of Assyria' (1996).
